Scaling and ideal points

Source: vignettes/scaling.Rmd
scaling.Rmd

Agreement scores and the scaling methods that place voters, judges or items on a line or in a plane.

Each section is one help page: what the function is for, the example of its help page as it runs, and the plot of its result where the package draws one. ?name gives the arguments and the value in full.

Vote agreement between legislators

votagr(): The share of the roll calls on which each pair of legislators (judges, council members) voted the same way, over the roll calls both took part in (Armstrong et al. 2021, section 3.2.2): the similarity matrix that metric scaling of a chamber starts from.

# five judges on eight simulated cases
set.seed(1)
v <- matrix(rbinom(40, 1, 0.5), 5, 8)
v[2, 3] <- NA
votagr(v)$agree
#>           [,1]      [,2]      [,3]      [,4]      [,5]
#> [1,] 1.0000000 0.5714286 0.5000000 0.6250000 0.2500000
#> [2,] 0.5714286 1.0000000 0.4285714 0.4285714 0.7142857
#> [3,] 0.5000000 0.4285714 1.0000000 0.3750000 0.5000000
#> [4,] 0.6250000 0.4285714 0.3750000 1.0000000 0.1250000
#> [5,] 0.2500000 0.7142857 0.5000000 0.1250000 1.0000000

Aldrich-McKelvey scaling

amscal(): Recovers the positions of stimuli (parties, candidates, courts) on one scale from respondents’ placements of them, each respondent allowed an own shift and stretch of the scale: z_{ij} = a_i + b_i z_j + epsilon_{ij}. The positions are the least-squares solution of Aldrich and McKelvey (1977): with X_i = [1, z_i] and P_i the projection onto its columns, z is the eigenvector of sum_i (I - P_i) with the smallest eigenvalue orthogonal to the constant. Respondents with a missing placement, or who place every stimulus at the same point, are left out of that sum. The positions are standardised to mean 0 and standard deviation 1, the first stimulus on the left. The respondent intercepts and slopes are each respondent’s least-squares regression of the placements on those positions (defined with two placements or more; a slope of zero is set to 1e-10).

# 40 simulated respondents place five stimuli on a 1-7 scale
set.seed(1)
truth <- c(-1.2, -0.4, 0.1, 0.9, 1.5)
Z <- t(vapply(1:40, function(i) {
  4 + rnorm(1, 0, 0.3) + runif(1, 0.6, 1.4) * truth + rnorm(5, 0, 0.3)
}, numeric(5)))
round(amscal(Z)$zhat, 2)
#> [1] -1.28 -0.59 -0.05  0.67  1.25
round((truth - mean(truth)) / sd(truth), 2)
#> [1] -1.30 -0.55 -0.08  0.68  1.24

Basic Space (blackbox) scaling

bbscal(): Recovers respondents’ positions from a respondent-by-issue matrix of responses by the decomposition of Poole (1998), X_0 = Psi W’ + J_n c’ + E_0 over the observed cells. Each dimension starts from the sign-corrected respondent means (column polarities from the pairwise correlations) and is refined by four alternating least-squares sweeps on the residuals of the earlier dimensions; up to five joint sweeps follow, stopping once the two half-step error sums of squares differ by less than 0.01; the fitted Psi W’ is then re-expressed by its singular value decomposition, Psi = U D^{1/2}, W = V D^{1/2}. Respondents with fewer than minscale responses are not scaled. The sign of each dimension is arbitrary.

# 30 simulated respondents on eight issues, ten answers missing
set.seed(1)
X <- matrix(rnorm(60), 30, 2) %*% matrix(rnorm(16), 2, 8) +
  matrix(rnorm(240, 0, 0.3), 30, 8)
X[sample(240, 10)] <- NA
bbscal(X, ndim = 2)$fit
#> [1] 0.9787813

Optimal Classification scaling

optcls(): Nonparametric ideal points from binary votes in the spirit of Poole (2000): each vote’s cutting direction is the unit-length difference of the mean positions of its yea and nay voters, each legislator moves to the mean of the directions of the sides taken, for maxit sweeps from each of nstart random starts; the start with the fewest classification errors is kept. A vote is split at the point of its direction that misclassifies fewest of its voters, either side voting yea, so no vote has more errors than voting with the majority.

# 20 simulated legislators, 30 votes cut along one dimension
set.seed(1)
x <- sort(rnorm(20))
v <- outer(x, rnorm(30), ">") * 1
optcls(v, maxit = 20, nstart = 2)$pre
#> [1] 1

Ordered Optimal Classification

ordocl(): Ordinal responses (a survey’s agree-disagree items, a court’s graded outcomes) classified by item directions and cutpoints in the spirit of Hare, Liu and Lupton (2018): respondents and item directions start normal (seed 42, as set.seed() takes it), the cutpoints of each item at equal steps on [-1, 1]; each sweep moves every cutpoint to the median of the midpoints between neighbouring respondents (in projection order) on either side of it, until the share classified correctly stops changing.

set.seed(1)
Y <- matrix(sample(1:4, 60, replace = TRUE), 15, 4)
ordocl(Y, ndim = 1, maxit = 20)$correct
#> [1] 0.2

Double-centre a distance matrix

dblctr(): B = - H D^{(2)} H with H = I - n^{-1} 1 1’ and D^{(2)} the squared distances: the inner-product matrix of classical scaling (Torgerson 1952).

D <- as.matrix(dist(cbind(c(0, 1, 3, 4), c(0, 1, 0, 2))))
dblctr(D)$B
#>         [,1]    [,2]    [,3]    [,4]
#> [1,]  4.5625  1.8125 -1.4375 -4.9375
#> [2,]  1.8125  1.0625 -1.1875 -1.6875
#> [3,] -1.4375 -1.1875  1.5625  1.0625
#> [4,] -4.9375 -1.6875  1.0625  5.5625

Classical (metric) multidimensional scaling

cmdsf(): Torgerson scaling: the leading eigenvectors of the double-centred squared distances (dblctr()), each scaled by the square root of its eigenvalue (negative ones set to 0). The fit is Mardia’s criterion, the kept positive eigenvalues over the sum of all absolute ones; the stress is Kruskal’s stress-1 against the positive distances. The sign of each dimension is arbitrary.

set.seed(1)
D <- as.matrix(dist(matrix(rnorm(40), 10)))
cmdsf(D)$fit
#> [1] 0.7816266

SMACOF stress minimisation

smacf(): Metric scaling by majorisation (de Leeuw 1977): each step is the Guttman transform X arrow V^{+} B(X) X with V = (W 1) - W, until the raw stress sum w_{ij} (d_{ij} - delta_{ij})^2 changes by less than tol.

set.seed(1)
D <- as.matrix(dist(matrix(rnorm(40), 10)))
smacf(D)$stress
#> [1] 6.626513

Nonmetric multidimensional scaling

nmdsf(): Kruskal’s nonmetric scaling: at each step the distances of the current configuration are fitted by a monotone (isotonic, pool-adjacent- violators) regression on the order of the dissimilarities, and one SMACOF step (smacf()) is taken towards the fitted disparities, until no coordinate moves by tol. The stress is Kruskal’s stress-1 of the last step. The start is normal from seed 42, as set.seed() takes it.

set.seed(1)
D <- as.matrix(dist(matrix(rnorm(40), 10)))
nmdsf(D, maxit = 50)$stress
#> [1] 0.1259758

Fit of a scaling by its eigenvalues

mdsfit(): Mardia’s criterion: the share of each dimension, its eigenvalue (0 when negative) over the sum of the absolute values of all eigenvalues, and the cumulative shares.

mdsfit(c(4, 2, 1, 0.5))
#> mdsfit:
#>   fit    0.53330 0.26670 0.13330 0.06667
#>   cumfit 0.5333 0.8000 0.9333 1.0000
#>   ev     4.0 2.0 1.0 0.5

INDSCAL: scaling with individual differences

indscl(): The weighted Euclidean model of Carroll and Chang (1970): one stimulus space shared by every individual, each individual weighting its dimensions. The configuration starts from classical scaling of the mean dissimilarities; then the weights of each individual and dimension (at least 0.01) and the stimulus coordinates are updated in turn until the configuration changes by a relative tol. The stress is the sum of squared differences between each individual’s dissimilarities and the distances in its weighted space.

set.seed(1)
D1 <- as.matrix(dist(matrix(rnorm(20), 5)))
D2 <- as.matrix(dist(matrix(rnorm(20), 5)))
indscl(list(D1, D2), maxit = 30)$weights
#>      [,1]    [,2]
#> [1,]   NA 1979597
#> [2,]   NA 1929755

Stress of an unfolding

unfstr(): The weighted sum of squared differences between the distances from respondents to stimuli in a configuration and the observed dissimilarities, over the observed cells.

set.seed(1)
unfstr(matrix(rnorm(6), 3), matrix(rnorm(8), 4), matrix(runif(12), 3))
#> unfstr:
#>   stress 32.263

Least-squares metric unfolding

mlsmu(): Unfolding of a respondent-by-stimulus matrix in the alternating least-squares form of MLSMU6 (Poole 1984): respondents and stimuli take gradient steps in turn against the row-centred dissimilarities, each step scaled by the largest eigenvalue of the gradient’s cross-product and both clouds centred, until the stress (unfstr()) changes by a relative tol; of nstart normal starts (seed 42, as set.seed() takes it) the lowest stress is kept.

set.seed(1)
D <- matrix(runif(120), 20, 6)
mlsmu(D, nstart = 1, maxit = 50)$stress
#> [1] 111.1204

SMACOF unfolding

smunf(): Unfolding by majorisation: respondents and stimuli are embedded in one space by SMACOF steps (smacf()) on the joint configuration with weight 1 between a respondent and a stimulus and 0 within each set (Borg and Groenen 2005, chapter 14). The start is normal from seed 42, as set.seed() takes it.

set.seed(1)
smunf(matrix(runif(12), 3), maxit = 20)$stress
#> [1] 3.242821

Ideal points from an unfolding

ipsrec(): In an unfolding the respondents’ coordinates are their ideal points (Armstrong et al. 2021, section 4.5): the respondent coordinates as a matrix.

set.seed(1)
u <- smunf(matrix(runif(12), 3), maxit = 20)
ipsrec(u$xr, u$xs)$ideal
#>            [,1]       [,2]
#> [1,] -0.4765297 -0.2645617
#> [2,] -0.3149654 -0.1746451
#> [3,] -0.4975857 -0.2764589

Procrustes rotation

procrs(): The orthogonal rotation (a proper rotation: no reflection) that best carries the centred configuration X onto the centred target in least squares, the target’s centre added back (Gower and Dijksterhuis 2004).

set.seed(1)
A <- matrix(rnorm(20), 10)
procrs(A, A %*% matrix(c(0, 1, -1, 0), 2))$rotation
#>      [,1]          [,2]
#> [1,]    0 -1.000000e+00
#> [2,]    1 -1.110223e-16

NOMINATE utilities and vote probabilities

nomutl(): The Gaussian utility of Poole and Rosenthal (1985): legislator i gains U = beta (- sum_k w_k^2 (x_{ik} - z_{jk})^2) from the outcome z_j; the probability of a yea is the logistic function of the yea utility minus the nay utility.

set.seed(1)
nomutl(matrix(rnorm(8), 4), matrix(rnorm(6), 3), matrix(rnorm(6), 3))$prob
#>             [,1]       [,2]         [,3]
#> [1,] 0.989937668 0.10357690 6.370307e-06
#> [2,] 0.990493247 0.99990393 4.484893e-02
#> [3,] 0.971693451 0.03457389 2.401618e-05
#> [4,] 0.008546933 0.05135459 2.061332e-02

One NOMINATE vote probability

nompr(): The probability of a yea of nomutl() for one legislator and one vote.

nompr(0.1, 0.3, -0.3)$prob
#> [1] 0.7018734

NOMINATE log-likelihood and classification

nomll(): The log-likelihood of the observed votes under the probabilities of nomutl() (clamped to [10^{-10}, 1 - 10^{-10}]) and gmp, the share of votes the model classifies correctly.

set.seed(1)
v <- matrix(rbinom(20, 1, 0.5), 4, 5)
nomll(v, matrix(rnorm(4)), matrix(rnorm(5)), matrix(rnorm(5)))
#> nomll:
#>   loglik  -48.178
#>   gmp     0.6
#>   correct 12
#>   total   20

DW-NOMINATE-style ideal points

dwnom(): A deterministic fixed-point fit in the Gaussian-utility family of Poole and Rosenthal (1997): from normal starts (seed 42, as set.seed() takes it), each vote’s normal vector and midpoint follow the mean positions of its two sides, and each legislator moves to the mean of the outcome locations (midpoint plus or minus half the normal) of the sides taken, the cloud shrunk into the unit ball, for maxit sweeps. The log-likelihood and the share classified correctly use the probit of the Gaussian utility difference with beta = 15 and equal dimension weights.

set.seed(1)
v <- matrix(rbinom(600, 1, 0.5), 20, 30)
dwnom(v, maxit = 20)$gmp
#> [1] 0.7033333

Parametric bootstrap of ideal points

nombt(): Standard errors of ideal points by the parametric bootstrap of Lewis and Poole (2004): votes are simulated from the fitted logistic probabilities (beta = 15 times the projection minus the cutpoint), absences kept, and each legislator re-estimated by 20 gradient steps from the fitted point plus normal noise of standard deviation 0.1. Draws come from seed, as set.seed() takes it.

set.seed(1)
v <- matrix(rbinom(40, 1, 0.5), 5, 8)
f <- dwnom(v, maxit = 5)
nombt(v, f$ideal, f$normals, f$cuts, nboot = 5)$se
#>            [,1]       [,2]
#> [1,] 0.03927144 0.08696910
#> [2,] 0.07038480 0.10135607
#> [3,] 0.08214763 0.11470586
#> [4,] 0.06887660 0.13162676
#> [5,] 0.13492223 0.07540698

Binary IRT likelihood

irtlik(): The log-likelihood of the votes under the probit item response model of Clinton, Jackman and Rivers (2004), P(y_{ij} = 1) = Phi(beta_j’ x_i - alpha_j) (clamped to [10^{-10}, 1 - 10^{-10}]), with the share of votes classified correctly.

set.seed(1)
v <- matrix(rbinom(20, 1, 0.5), 4, 5)
irtlik(v, matrix(rnorm(4)), rep(0, 5), matrix(rnorm(5)))$loglik
#> [1] -22.8751

EM estimation of binary IRT ideal points

irtem(): The EM algorithm of Imai, Lo and Olmsted (2016) for the probit model y^{ij} = alpha_j + beta_j’ x_i + e{ij}, yea when y^_{ij} > 0, with priors x_i N(mu_x, s^2_x I) and (alpha_j, beta_j) N(mu_b, s^2_b I). The E-step replaces y^* by its truncated-normal mean (untruncated when absent); the M-step is the pair of ridge regressions; the fixed point is the posterior mode. The default start is alpha = beta = 0 and x from 50 steps of orthogonal iteration on the cross-product of the column-centred +1/-1 votes.

set.seed(1)
x <- rnorm(20)
v <- matrix(rbinom(600, 1, pnorm(outer(x, rnorm(30)))), 20)
cor(irtem(v)$ideal[, 1], x)
#> [1] 0.8854776

Posterior summaries of ideal-point draws

irtpst(): Means, standard deviations and central 95% intervals (R’s default quantile, type 7) of a chain of ideal points, each draw first standardised dimension by dimension when std is TRUE (location and scale are not identified in IRT models; Jackman 2009).

set.seed(1)
irtpst(array(rnorm(100 * 5 * 2), c(100, 5, 2)))$mean
#>             [,1]         [,2]
#> [1,]  0.06747061 -0.008652293
#> [2,] -0.06792212 -0.144214340
#> [3,]  0.01295946  0.064296854
#> [4,]  0.07157441  0.079645425
#> [5,] -0.08408237  0.008924354

Clinton-Jackman-Rivers Bayesian IRT

cjrirt(): The probit ideal-point model P(y_{ij} = 1) = Phi(beta_j’ x_i - alpha_j) with priors x_i N(0, I) and (alpha_j, beta_j) N(0, v I) (Clinton, Jackman and Rivers 2004), by the Gibbs sampler of Albert and Chib (1993): latent utilities from truncated normals, then every (alpha_j, beta_j) and every x_i from its normal full conditional. Every draw is an inverse normal of a uniform of Philox4x32-10 (Salmon et al. 2011), sweep t on stream t of key seed, so a chain is the same on every platform. The default start is the posterior mode of irtem().

votes <- rbind(c(1, 1, 0, 0), c(1, 1, 1, 0), c(0, 1, 1, 1),
               c(0, 0, 1, 1), c(1, 0, 0, 0))
round(cjrirt(votes, nsamp = 50, burn = 10)$ideal, 3)
#>        [,1]
#> [1,] -1.209
#> [2,] -0.508
#> [3,]  0.358
#> [4,]  0.859
#> [5,] -0.904

Bayesian Aldrich-McKelvey scaling

bamscl(): Respondent i places stimulus j at z_{ij} N(a_i + b_i z_j, 1 / (tau_i tau_j)): a respondent’s shift and stretch of the common positions z, with noise whose precision factors into a respondent and a stimulus part (Hare et al. 2015). Priors: a_i, b_i U(-100, 100), tau_j G(0.1, 0.1), tau_i G(g_a, g_b) with g_a, g_b G(0.1, 0.1), and z the standardised z^* N(0, 1), the polarity stimulus restricted to the left. Gibbs sampling: a_i and b_i from truncated normals, the precisions and g_b from conjugate gammas, g_a and each z^*_j by slice sampling (Neal 2003). Draws come from seed, as set.seed() takes it; rows with no placement are dropped.

# 40 simulated respondents place four stimuli
set.seed(1)
zt <- c(-1, -0.3, 0.4, 1.2)
Z <- rnorm(40, 0, 0.5) + outer(runif(40, 0.5, 1.5), zt) +
  matrix(rnorm(160, 0, 0.3), 40, 4)
round(bamscl(Z, nsamp = 100, burn = 50)$zeta, 2)
#> [1] -1.14 -0.42  0.40  1.16

Bayesian metric multidimensional scaling

bmdsf(): Each observed dissimilarity is lognormal about the distance between the two objects’ coordinates, delta_{ij} N(d_{ij}, 1 / tau), with x_{ik} N(0, 10^2) and tau U(0, 10) (Bakker and Poole 2013). Coordinates are slice sampled one at a time (Neal 2003), tau drawn from its truncated gamma; the chain starts from classical scaling plus small normal noise. The likelihood is unchanged by translation, rotation and reflection, so every draw is aligned (translation and rotation) onto the posterior mean. Zero, negative or missing dissimilarities are left out. Draws come from seed, as set.seed() takes it.

set.seed(1)
D <- as.matrix(dist(matrix(rnorm(16), 8)))
f <- bmdsf(D, nsamp = 50, burn = 50)
cor(f$dist[upper.tri(D)], D[upper.tri(D)])
#> [1] 0.9757443

Bayesian unfolding

bunfld(): The lognormal model of bmdsf() for a respondent-by-stimulus matrix: delta_{ij} N(x_i - z_j , 1 / tau), N(0, 10^2) priors on every coordinate and tau U(0, 10) (Bakker and Poole 2013). Feeling thermometers T on 0-100 enter as delta = (100 - T) / 50. Given the stimuli the respondents are independent, and the other way round, so each block is slice sampled at once, dimension by dimension; draws are aligned on the stimuli. The chain starts from the singular value decomposition of the centred matrix. Draws come from seed, as set.seed() takes it.

set.seed(1)
S <- matrix(runif(8, -0.5, 0.5), 4)
R <- matrix(runif(60, -0.5, 0.5), 30)
D <- sqrt(outer(R[, 1], S[, 1], "-")^2 + outer(R[, 2], S[, 2], "-")^2)
f <- bunfld(D, nsamp = 50, burn = 50)
cor(as.numeric(f$dist), as.numeric(D))
#> [1] 0.9766247

Alpha-NOMINATE

anomin(): Legislator i votes yea on roll call j with probability Phi(u_{ij}), u_{ij} = Q_{ij} + alpha (G_{ij} - Q_{ij}), where Q is the quadratic and G the Gaussian utility difference of the distances to the yea and nay outcomes, with weight 0.5 (Carroll et al. 2013): alpha = 1 is Gaussian utility, alpha = 0 quadratic. beta has a flat prior on (0, Inf), alpha on [0, 1]; coordinates carry the hierarchical penalty -x’Sx/2 with S redrawn each sweep from an inverse Wishart. Every coordinate, beta and alpha are slice sampled (Neal 2003: width 8, at most 3 steps out); starts are uniform on (-1, 1), beta = 10, alpha = 0.7. Each draw is then centred on its legislators and rotated onto the posterior mean, the polarity legislator positive. Roll calls whose minority side is below lop and legislators with fewer than minvotes votes are dropped first. Draws come from seed, as set.seed() takes it.

# 20 simulated legislators on a line, 30 roll calls, some votes flipped
set.seed(1)
x <- seq(-1, 1, length.out = 20)
V <- outer(x, runif(30, -0.7, 0.7), ">") * 1
flip <- sample(length(V), 30)
V[flip] <- 1 - V[flip]
f <- anomin(V, nsamp = 20, burn = 10, minvotes = 10, polarity = 20)
f$alpha
#> [1] 0.9071232

Ordinal IRT (ordinal factor model)

ordirt(): Each ordinal response is a thresholded latent normal, y^{ij} = lambda{j0} + lambda_j’ phi_i + e_{ij}, y_{ij} = c when gamma_{j,c-1} < y^_{ij} <= gamma_{j,c}, with gamma_{j1} = 0, phi_i N(0, I), loadings lambda_j N(0, I / L_0) and a flat prior on the free cutpoints (Quinn 2004). Each sweep updates the free cutpoints of every item by the Metropolis-Hastings step of Cowles (1996) with y^* integrated out (step sizes tuned during the burn-in only), then draws y^*, the loadings and the ideal points from their full conditionals. The chain starts from the leading principal components of the mean-filled responses. Each draw is reflected so the first item loads positively (rotated onto the first draw with several dimensions). Draws come from seed, as set.seed() takes it.

set.seed(1)
th <- rnorm(60)
Y <- matrix(cut(outer(th, runif(6, 0.8, 1.5)) + rnorm(360),
                c(-Inf, -0.5, 0.5, Inf), labels = FALSE), 60, 6)
f <- ordirt(Y, nsamp = 50, burn = 50)
cor(f$ideal[, 1], th)
#> [1] 0.8995402

Dynamic IRT (ideal points that drift)

dynirt(): The one-dimensional dynamic item response model of Martin and Quinn (2002), made for courts: a vote is cast when z_{jk} = -alpha_k + beta_k theta_{j,t(k)} + {jk} > 0; the ideal points follow a random walk, theta{j,0} N(e_0, E_0), theta_{j,t} N(theta_{j,t-1}, tau^2_j); alpha_k N(a_0, 1/A_0), beta_k N(b_0, 1/B_0). Each sweep draws the latent utilities, every case’s (alpha, beta), every justice’s path by forward filtering and backward sampling and, when c0 and d0 are positive, the evolution variances from IG((c_0 + T)/2, (d_0 + SS)/2). A draw is reflected whenever the anchor member’s mean ideal point is negative. The chain starts from the first principal component of the votes. Draws come from seed, as set.seed() takes it.

# 12 simulated justices over three terms of 15 cases
set.seed(7)
period <- rep(1:3, each = 15)
walk <- function(s) s + cumsum(c(0, rnorm(2, 0, 0.3)))
truth <- t(vapply(rnorm(12), walk, numeric(3)))
p <- pnorm(-rep(rnorm(45, 0, 0.5), each = 12) +
  rep(rnorm(45, 1.5, 0.5), each = 12) * truth[, period])
V <- matrix(rbinom(length(p), 1, p), 12)
f <- dynirt(V, period, nsamp = 100, burn = 50)
cor(as.numeric(f$theta), as.numeric(truth))
#> [1] 0.9013526

Anchoring vignettes

anchv(): Corrects self-ratings for differential item functioning with anchoring vignettes, nonparametrically (King et al. 2004): each respondent’s ratings of the vignettes, sorted, give that respondent’s thresholds between categories, and the self-rating is recoded as the number of thresholds at or below it. The spread of each threshold across respondents measures the differential item functioning.

set.seed(1)
anchv(sample(1:5, 30, TRUE), matrix(sample(1:5, 90, TRUE), 30))$dif
#> [1] 1.0618786 1.0618786 1.2429109 0.8193072

Bootstrap of scaling positions

scboot(): Standard errors and percentile intervals of Aldrich-McKelvey stimulus positions (amscal()) or Basic Space weights (bbscal(), first dimension, of the matrix or of its transpose) by resampling respondents with replacement (Efron and Tibshirani 1993). Draws come from seed, as set.seed() takes it. The sign of a Basic Space dimension is arbitrary, so its replicates are best compared after aligning them.

set.seed(1)
Z <- matrix(rnorm(100), 20, 5) + rep(1:5, each = 20)
scboot(Z, nboot = 10)$se
#> [1] 0.09685089 0.13563335 0.07232775 0.09721725 0.07797385

Normal vector of an outside measure

nrmvec(): Projects an outside measure (a judge’s party, a legislator’s vote share) into an ideal-point space: the least-squares regression of the measure on the coordinates, its slopes scaled to unit length give the direction along which the measure rises, with its angle and the R^2 (Armstrong et al. 2021, section 2.6).

set.seed(1)
nrmvec(matrix(rnorm(20), 10), rnorm(10))$degrees
#> [1] 153.4453

Cutting lines of votes in two dimensions

cutlns(): The ends of each vote’s cutting line n_1 x + n_2 y = c across the horizontal range xlim (or from -10 to 10 vertically when the line is vertical), its midpoint and the angle of its normal: the lines of a Coombs mesh (Poole 2005). The plot itself is not drawn here.

set.seed(1)
cutlns(matrix(rnorm(6), 3), c(0.1, -0.2, 0))$ends
#>      [,1]        [,2] [,3]       [,4]
#> [1,]   -1 -0.33000699    1  0.4553768
#> [2,]   -1 -0.04963973    1 -1.1642922
#> [3,]   -1  1.01847753    1 -1.0184775

Wordfish: positions from word counts

wrdfsh(): The Poisson scaling model of Slapin and Proksch (2008), y_{ij} ((psi_i + alpha_j + beta_j omega_i)), for documents (judgments, briefs, platforms) by their word counts: alternating Newton steps on the document positions omega (standardised after each sweep, the word parameters adjusted to keep the linear predictor) and on the word parameters, from normal starts (seed 42, as set.seed() takes it), until the positions change by a relative tol. The sign of the scale is arbitrary.

set.seed(1)
wrdfsh(matrix(rpois(600, 5), 20), maxit = 20)$pos

#>  [8] -0.83530154 -0.99936159  0.25353260 -0.31732379 -1.84826884 -0.20769336  1.06437931
